summary: DHCP gives IPv4 hosts addressing and configuration information. This informational RFC discusses the identifiers DHCP carries and the privacy problems they may cause, such as letting observers recognize and track a device.

plainLanguage.summary: When a computer joins a network, it tells its name and ID number. This explains how those details can be used to follow it around.

subtitle: How DHCP reveals device identities and enables tracking

tldr.problem: DHCP is used to assign IP addresses and configuration to devices when they join a network. The protocol carries several stable identifiers (MAC address, client ID, hostname, vendor information) that can be observed by network eavesdroppers and used to track devices across networks, discover their type and operating system, and infer their location.
tldr.mechanism: This document identifies the DHCP options and fields that leak identifying information, describes practical attacks that use this information (device fingerprinting, location tracking, correlation over time), and explains how existing mechanisms like DNS updates and allocation strategies either help or harm privacy.
tldr.outcome: The document does not propose fixes (those are left to future work) but serves as an analysis to inform future protocol design. It highlights that client authentication and privacy are in tension: proving who you are reveals who you are.

today: RFC 7819 remains the authoritative analysis of DHCP privacy issues. It is informational and does not obsolete or update any standards. Future protocol work may build on the issues identified here. Related privacy work in IETF has continued, including privacy extensions for DHCPv6 and emphasis on encryption (e.g., DNS over HTTPS) to reduce eavesdropping opportunities. Device manufacturers and network operators can use this analysis to understand the privacy implications of their DHCP deployments.

sections.title: DHCP Identifiers and Privacy Risks
sections.content:
The Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) is used to automatically assign IP addresses and network settings to devices (clients) when they connect to a network. The protocol works by having a device broadcast a request, and a DHCP server responds with an address and configuration information.

DHCP messages carry several pieces of identifying information: the device's hardware (MAC) address, a client identifier (often derived from the MAC address or a stable ID stored on the device), the device's hostname, the vendor class (identifying manufacturer), and the list of options the client is requesting. An eavesdropper on the network—or an operator controlling an access point—can observe all of this information and use it to identify, fingerprint, and track devices.

This is particularly problematic in mobile scenarios: a laptop or phone that connects to many different networks (home, work, coffee shops, airports) will repeatedly send the same identifiers, allowing each network to recognize the device as the same one that visited before, and potentially to correlate the device's activities across unrelated networks.
sections.plainLanguage: DHCP sends a device's name, ID, and type to the network. Anyone listening can recognize the device again later, even on different networks.

sections.title: Identifying Information in DHCP
sections.content:
Several DHCP options and fields carry identifying data:

Client Identifier: Typically contains the device's MAC address (hardware address) or a stable ID. It is expected to remain the same across reboots and is unique within a subnet. Even if a device later randomizes its MAC address, the client identifier may still contain the original address.

Hardware Address (chaddr): The MAC address field in the DHCP message header, used both for routing replies and as an identifier.

Hostname (FQDN Option): The device's fully qualified domain name. A device called "alice-laptop" is easily correlated with Alice across networks.

Vendor Class and Vendor Information: Opaque fields identifying the device manufacturer and software version. These allow an attacker to guess the device type and operating system, enabling targeted exploits.

Parameter Request List: The list of options the client asks the server to provide. Different devices (phones vs laptops, different OSes) request different options, creating a fingerprint.

Relay Agent Information: Added by network infrastructure, can contain circuit IDs, remote IDs, and subscriber IDs that correlate to physical locations or customer identities.
sections.plainLanguage: DHCP messages can include: the device's MAC address, a client ID (often the same as MAC), the hostname, the vendor name and version, the list of options it wants, and location hints from the network.

sections.title: Practical Privacy Attacks Using DHCP Information
sections.content:
Device Type Discovery: An attacker observes the Vendor Class option, the MAC address OUI (Organizationally Unique Identifier, which identifies the manufacturer), and the client ID to guess the device type (e.g., Apple iPhone, Dell laptop). This enables targeted attacks against vulnerabilities specific to that device.

Operating System Fingerprinting: The combination of options in the Parameter Request List, the Vendor Class, and the System Architecture Type option reveal hints about the OS. Different versions of Windows, macOS, iOS, and Linux request different options.

Location Tracking: If the relay agent information includes a circuit ID or link-selection suboption that corresponds to a physical location, or if a civic location option is returned by the server, an attacker learns where the device is. Even without explicit location data, a device's IP address can often be mapped to a location.

Finding Previously Visited Networks: A device trying to rejoin a network it has visited before includes the previously assigned IP address in a "requested IP address" option. By observing these requests, an attacker can infer which networks a device has previously visited.

Correlation Over Time: Stable identifiers like client ID, hostname, or MAC address allow an attacker to track the same device across multiple sessions on the same network or even across different networks if the identifier does not change.

Leasequery Attacks: Attackers can query DHCP servers (using mechanisms designed for operators) to obtain detailed binding information about devices, including their hardware addresses, assigned addresses, and location information.
sections.plainLanguage: An attacker watching DHCP can learn: what device it is, what OS it runs, where it is, where it has been, and how to follow it around by recognizing its stable ID.

sections.title: Existing Mechanisms and Their Privacy Effects
sections.content:
DNS Updates: When DHCP is combined with DNS Update mechanisms, the DHCP server can automatically insert the device's hostname and assigned address into the DNS. This makes the mapping between hostname (e.g., "alice-laptop") and current IP address publicly queryable. DNS queries are often logged; anyone can query to discover a device's current address and correlate that with web server logs or other activity traces.

Address Allocation Strategies: How a server assigns addresses affects privacy:

Iterative allocation assigns addresses in sequence, making addresses predictable and enabling scanning attacks. Identifier-based allocation derives the address from the client's stable ID, so the same client always gets the same address, enabling correlation and location tracking. Random allocation assigns unpredictable addresses, better for privacy but offers no guarantee that a returning client gets the same address. Hash-based allocation derives addresses from a hash of the ID, which can obscure the identifier if the hash is strong.

In the IPv4 address space (which is much smaller than IPv6), the choice of allocation strategy has less impact on privacy than in IPv6, where address pools are enormous.
sections.plainLanguage: DNS updates put device names and addresses into a public directory. Address assignment strategies affect whether the same device always gets the same address (predictable, easy to track) or a random one each time (harder to track).

sections.title: Security vs. Privacy and Next Steps
sections.content:
A fundamental tension exists between client authentication and privacy. To prove a client is who it claims to be, the client must reveal identifying information (credentials, certificates, stable identifiers). Full privacy—where no one, not even the network operator, knows who you are—is incompatible with authentication.

This document analyzes the privacy issues but does not propose solutions. Future work may suggest protocol changes to reduce identifier leakage, support optional privacy modes, or enable encryption of DHCP exchanges. Some solutions might include:

Randomizing or obfuscating MAC addresses and client IDs, reducing what information clients put in the parameter request list, separating client authentication from network access, or encrypting DHCP messages between client and server.

The document also notes that the primary focus is on client privacy (since clients are mobile and vulnerable), while server and relay agent privacy is considered less critical (they provide public services and communicate over protected backbone links).
sections.plainLanguage: To prove you are who you say you are, you have to reveal your identity. True privacy means being anonymous, which conflicts with authentication. Future fixes will have to balance these tradeoffs.
